newsitem.title: USA: Difficult road seen for increase in Russia aid.
newsitem.headline: Difficult road seen for increase in Russia aid.

text.p: A key member of the House told the Clinton administration on Tuesday that it faced a tough task to persuade Congress to support a sharp increase in aid to Russia.

The administration wants to increase the Russian aid level to $242 million in the fiscal year starting on Oct. 1, from $95 million in the current year. The new aid request is part of a $900 million package for the 12 former Soviet states.

"Such an increase comes at a time when many in the Congress are seriously troubled by the trends in Russian foreign policy," Republican Representative Benjamin Gilman, of New York, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, said.

He told administration witnesses there was also concern about allegations that a Russian aid increase might be part of a package of "concessions" offered in response to Russian objections to expansion of the NATO alliance.

Gilman, whose committee is due to draft a foreign aid authorisation bill, criticised Russian policies, including charges it was continuing to develop chemical and biological weapons, and said: "We do not have any kind of 'partnership' at this point with the current government in Moscow.
"Accordingly, gentlemen, I believe that you have your job cut out for you in persuading members of Congress to support increased aid to Russia."

Representative Doug Bereuter, a Nebraska Republican, questioned an administration plan under which the government's Export-Import Bank, which helps facilitate U.S. exports, would operate in former Soviet states.
He said he was concerned about enlarging the bank's role, calling it one of the "dumbest" decisions to come from the administration.

Aid coordinator Richard Morningstar defended the plan as a way to bring U.S. exports into the region but said the administration could find other ways to help small businesses in the region if the idea was unacceptable.

Morningstar and Thomas Dine, an Agency for International Development official, defended aid to Russia as being in U.S. national security interests by helping to promote democracy and market reforms in the region.
They said the reforms were starting to bring results but Morningstar said there was a question of whether aid would continue to Belarus, which he said "has probably been the biggest disappointment."
